title: EY, Deloitte and a Space Startup All Opened AI Centres in Bengaluru This Week. The Pattern Is Clear.
excerpt: Three separate investments in one city in five days signal that India's tech capital is becoming the world's AI back office — with implications for every Indian technologist abroad
body:
In the span of five days, three major players announced AI investments in Bengaluru: EY opened a 40,000 square-foot AI centre backed by a $1.4 billion global AI budget; Deloitte India inaugurated a dedicated SAP-focused AI delivery hub; and Indian space startup SatSure secured a ₹246 crore ($2.6 million) government grant to build sovereign AI models for Earth observation. Together, they tell a story that has been building for years but is now undeniable: Bengaluru is no longer just India's IT outsourcing capital. It is becoming the world's AI back office.

## The EY Play

EY's new AI centre will focus on helping enterprises test and scale AI-led transformation across life sciences, industrial products, consumer goods, and energy. The facility is part of the firm's broader $1.4 billion investment in artificial intelligence, which includes embedding AI into its proprietary platforms and developing EY.ai EYQ, a large language model used internally by EY teams worldwide.

The centre will create specialised roles in AI engineering, immersive experience design, and digital twin modelling — the kind of work that was, until recently, done almost exclusively in New York, London, or San Francisco.

EY says over 83% of its employees have completed foundational AI learning, with 115,000 AI-related badges issued. The Bengaluru centre will be the hub where that trained workforce meets live enterprise problems.

## Deloitte and SAP Join Forces

Deloitte India's new SAP Delivery Centre, also in Bengaluru, is designed to support SAP's transformation priorities and help enterprises accelerate cloud adoption, intelligent automation, and AI-powered business processes. Supported by an ecosystem of more than 1,000 professionals across India, the centre will cover the full lifecycle from innovation and architecture to implementation and managed evolution.

This is one of Deloitte's first strategic SAP-focused delivery centres in India — a signal that the firm sees Bengaluru not just as a cost arbitrage play but as a genuine centre of technical excellence for enterprise AI.

## The Sovereign AI Bet

SatSure's story is different but complementary. The Bengaluru-based geospatial analytics firm received its ₹246 crore grant from India's space regulator, IN-SPACe, to develop large Earth observation models using satellite and drone data tailored specifically to Indian conditions.

"Earth observation is moving from project-specific analytics to reusable intelligence infrastructure," said SatSure co-founder Rashmit Singh Sukhmani. The models will cover monsoon patterns, agricultural landscapes, and urban expansion — areas where global AI models often struggle with local accuracy.

The grant is part of India's 10-billion-rupee fund to help space startups scale up, reflecting a broader government push to build sovereign AI capabilities and reduce dependence on foreign technology platforms.

## The Bigger Pattern

The three announcements did not happen in coordination, which makes their convergence more meaningful, not less. They reflect a structural shift: multinationals are no longer just hiring Indian engineers remotely. They are building centres of gravity in Bengaluru, where the combination of deep technical talent, lower costs, and proximity to the world's fastest-growing major economy creates a gravitational pull that is difficult to resist.

TCS's partnership with Anthropic, announced the same week, adds another data point. The company will equip 50,000 associates with Anthropic's Claude AI tools and jointly take AI solutions to market for regulated sectors. TCS chairman N. Chandrasekaran said the company expects to move toward having an equal number of employees and AI agents in its workforce.

## What It Means for Indians Abroad

For the hundreds of thousands of Indian technologists working in the US and UK, the implications are direct. Bengaluru's AI hiring boom is creating roles — AI engineering leads, digital twin architects, immersive experience designers — that pay well by Indian standards and offer the kind of cutting-edge work that once required a Silicon Valley address.

The reverse brain drain that Indian policymakers have talked about for decades may finally have an economic engine behind it. The question is no longer whether Bengaluru can compete for AI talent. It is whether the city's infrastructure — its roads, its housing, its schools — can keep up with the ambition its tech sector is now projecting to the world.
